title: The characteristic polynomial
summary: Turn Av = λv into det(A − λI) = 0, expand it for a 2×2, and solve it with the trace and determinant.

blocks.title: Collect v on one side

define.meaning: $I = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$. It leaves every vector as it is: $Iv = v$.
$A$ with $\lambda$ taken off each diagonal entry. The other entries stay.

blocks.why: $Av = \lambda v$ has $v$ on both sides. Writing $\lambda v$ as $\lambda I v$ lets you collect it: $(A - \lambda I)\,v = 0$, one matrix times $v$.

slips.say: $3I$ has 3 on the diagonal and 0 off it. Only the diagonal of $A$ changes.

hints: Subtract entry by entry. Off the diagonal you subtract 0.
The diagonal entries become $2 - 3$; the off-diagonal ones stay as in $A$.

check.say: Multiply your matrix by $(1, 1)$. Since $A\,(1, 1) = 3\,(1, 1)$, you should get $(0, 0)$.

blocks.solution: $(A - 3I)\,(1, 1) = (0, 0)$: the eigenvector from lesson 1 is sent to zero. That is $Av = \lambda v$ rewritten.

blocks.title: Its determinant

define.meaning: A square $M$ sends some non-zero $v$ to 0 exactly when $\det M = 0$ (then $M$ has no inverse).

blocks.why: You don't know $v$ yet. The determinant tests whether a non-zero $v$ with $(A - \lambda I)\,v = 0$ exists, without finding it.

slips.say: $ad - bc$: the off-diagonal product is subtracted. $(-1)(-1) - 1 \cdot 1$.

hints: $ad - bc$, with $a$ and $d$ on the diagonal.

check.say: It must come out so that a non-zero $v$ can exist: you already know one, $(1, 1)$.

blocks.solution: 0, as it must be. Compare $\lambda = 4$: $A - 4I = \begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $4 - 1 = 3 \ne 0$, so 4 is not an eigenvalue. The eigenvalues are exactly the $\lambda$ that make $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.
blocks.next: Expand it with λ left in

blocks.title: Expand det(B − λI)

define.meaning: $\det(A - \lambda I)$, written out as a polynomial in $\lambda$. Its roots are the eigenvalues.

blocks.why: Keep $\lambda$ as an unknown and the determinant becomes a quadratic. Its roots are every eigenvalue at once.
blocks.prompt: Let $B = \begin{bmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$. Expand $\det(B - \lambda I)$ as a polynomial in $\lambda$. Type $\lambda$ as the letter x.

slips.say: The off-diagonal product $1 \cdot 2$ was added. In $ad - bc$ it is subtracted.

check.say: Put $\lambda = 0$ into your polynomial: you should get $\det B = 4 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 2$.

blocks.solution: $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10$. Look at the 7 and the 10: both come straight from $B$.

blocks.title: Trace and determinant

define.meaning: $\operatorname{tr}(A)$, the sum of the diagonal entries: $a + d$ for $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$.

blocks.why: For every $2 \times 2$, $\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - \operatorname{tr}(A)\,\lambda + \det(A)$. So two numbers give you the whole polynomial.

slips.say: That adds all four entries. The trace is the diagonal only: $4 + 3$.
$ad - bc$: subtract the off-diagonal product $1 \cdot 2$, don't add it.
That is the other diagonal, $1 + 2$. The trace runs top-left to bottom-right: $4 + 3$.

hints: The trace uses the two entries on the diagonal from top-left to bottom-right.

check.say: Compare with your polynomial $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10$: the trace is the number after the minus sign, the determinant is the constant.

blocks.solution: Why it works: $(a - \lambda)(d - \lambda) - bc = \lambda^2 - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc)$.

blocks.title: From Av = λv to a quadratic
blocks.why: This chain is the whole method. Putting it in order checks that each line really follows from the one before.
blocks.prompt: Put these in order, from the definition of an eigenvector to the equation for a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$.

items.text: Write $\lambda v$ as $\lambda I v$: then $Av - \lambda I v = 0$.
Both terms are a matrix times $v$, so $(A - \lambda I)\,v = 0$.
That matrix sends a non-zero $v$ to 0, so it has no inverse.
So its determinant is zero: $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$.

say.insert-identity: What must happen to $\lambda v$ before it can be subtracted from $Av$?
say.factor: You can only take $v$ out once both terms are a matrix times $v$. What makes $\lambda v$ a matrix times $v$?
say.not-invertible: This line is about a matrix sending $v$ to 0. Which line gives that matrix?
say.determinant: A determinant of zero is the test for a matrix with no inverse. What must come before it?
say.quadratic: This expands a determinant. Which line sets the determinant to zero?

blocks.hint: Each line uses the object the line above it produced: first $\lambda I v$, then $A - \lambda I$, then its determinant.
blocks.solution: The eigenvalues are the roots of $\det(A - \lambda I)$, and for a $2 \times 2$ that is $\lambda^2 - \operatorname{tr}(A)\,\lambda + \det(A)$.

blocks.title: The eigenvalues of B
blocks.why: The roots of the characteristic polynomial are the eigenvalues. Now you can find them without guessing a single vector.
blocks.prompt: $B = \begin{bmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$, with $\det(B - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10$. Find its eigenvalues, largest first.

slips.say: $(\lambda - 5)(\lambda - 2) = 0$ is solved by $\lambda = 5$ and $\lambda = 2$: the signs flip when you move them across.

check.say: The two eigenvalues add up to the trace (7) and multiply to the determinant (10).

blocks.solution: $\lambda = 5$ and $\lambda = 2$. They add to $\operatorname{tr}(B)$ and multiply to $\det(B)$, which is always true for a $2 \times 2$.

blocks.title: Back to A
blocks.why: In lesson 1 you found the eigenvalues of $A$ by testing vectors. The shortcut should give the same two numbers with no vectors at all.
blocks.prompt: Use $\lambda^2 - \operatorname{tr}(A)\,\lambda + \det(A) = 0$ to find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, largest first.
hints: Two numbers that add to 4 and multiply to 3.
blocks.solution: 3 and 1, the stretches you saw in lesson 1. The polynomial finds the eigenvalues; next lesson finds the vectors that go with them.
